extracted.intended_audience: general news readers and newswire editors
extracted.subtask_description: Associated Press-style newswire reporting of Cold War-era events (atomic tests, civil defense, diplomatic conferences), intended for rapid distribution to newspapers and broadcasters. Includes timed/embargoed copy and embedded technical and policy details for public and official audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance/embargo labeling for wire copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire stories include explicit 'advance' or embargo markers indicating the authorized time for publication or broadcast (e.g., '(ADVANCE FOR USE AT 9 P.M. EST TODAY, FEB. 22)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: '(ADVANCE FOR USE AT 9 P.M. EST TODAY, FEB. 22)', '(ADVANCE) ... (ADVANCE FOR USE AT 8 P.M. EST, TUESDAY, FEB 22)'. These tags are used to control distribution/timing of release by subscribing outlets and should be preserved and respected when republishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of smoke screens to reduce thermal radiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A blanket of artificial smoke can help save towns and cities from the searing, flashing heat of an atomic bomb by attenuating thermal radiation, though it will not stop blast or gamma radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two types of smoke identified: a fog-oil 'smog' of oil droplets and carbon smoke (carbon smoke may be even more effective). Smoke should be below the level of a bomb burst; a smoke-screen layer should be no higher than 1,000 to 2,000 feet. Weather and wind conditions are critical (they determine screen height); 'exhaustive studies' are needed for potential target areas (more than 100 areas mentioned). Smoke can be produced by industrial plants and home oil-heating plants without special equipment. Note the limitation: smoke does not stop blast or gamma radiation; it may reduce secondary fires and thermal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated damage radii and effects for planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Published numerical estimates of damage radii and dominant effects for an atomic explosion of a given explosive equivalent (example cited: 'explosive equivalent of 20,000 tons of TNT').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives planning-use figures (as reported): 'area of complete ... a half-mile', 'buildings destroyed up to one mile', and that gamma radiation from a burst at 2,000-foot altitude 'extends to about three-fourths of a [mile]' (text is garbled but provides concrete distance estimates). These empirical estimates (and casualty timing observations from Hiroshima/Nagasaki: 20–30% of fatal casualties in first second; burns accounted for more than half) are presented as the basis for civil-defense planning and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedoms Foundation award selection emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Freedoms Foundation citations honor 'contributions of 1954 to the ... American way' and recognize citizens, organizations and schools for actions 'to further the American way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prizes are awarded to first-place winners and special award recipients drawn from a large field (text notes over 100,000 entries). Monetary and special awards are part of the program (the story cites $14,000 total in prize awards and two special awards of $1,000 each). The foundation is described as non-political, non-sectarian, seeking to honor citizens for things they 'say, do and write' that further its aims.
